entries.title: Man charged in fatal late-night Lake View beating
entries.summary: <p>A man has been charged in the fatal beating of another man in Lake View, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Mateusz Mysliwiec, 35, was arrested Sunday on a charge of first-degree murder, police said.</p><p>Mysliwiec is alleged to have killed a 51-year-old man in the 800 block of West Wellington Avenue just before midnight on Oct. 2, police said.</p><p>He is due in court again Wednesday.</p>

entries.title: Former CPS employees plead guilty to federal fraud charges in district contract kickback scheme
entries.summary: <p>A former Chicago Public Schools principal and an ex-CPS employee plead guilty to fraud in federal court for their roles in a kickback scheme that took thousands from local school districts, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Illinois.</p><p>Antonio Ross and Alfonzo Lewis both signed plea deals Tuesday after being <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/09/ex-superintendent-of-evanston-skokie-school-district-65-at-center-of-federal-corruption-indictment" target="_blank" ><u>indicted</u></a><u> </u>just over a year ago, according to court records.</p><p>The two allegedly created companies to apply as vendors for professional service contracts with District 65, submitting “false and fraudulent” documents to win them and then hid thousands of dollars in kickbacks to then-district superintendent Devon Horton, according to prosecutors.</p><p>Ross, then serving as Hyde Park Academy High School principal, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/09/ex-superintendent-of-evanston-skokie-school-district-65-at-center-of-federal-corruption-indictment" target="_blank" ><u>obtained nearly $120,000 from District 65</u></a> and paid Horton nearly $42,000 from the proceeds, prosecutors said. </p><p>The scheme ran from August 2020 to June 2023, court entries.title: Chicago Park District said Griffin MSI's planned Welcome Hall is too big before supporting project anyway
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Park District asked the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry to shrink the size of the 458-foot long, two-story Welcome Hall that's planned for the institution’s main entry — but later supported the design after consulting with preservationists in the government and local nonprofit fields.</p><p>The Welcome Hall, which would be located outside the historic building’s North Portico, “quickly rises to a height that visually blocks the lower portions of the historic facades from most vantage points beyond the corners of the original courtyard,” Chicago Park District Planning and Research Manager Nelson Chueng wrote in a March 24 letter to Griffin MSI's Vice President of Government Affairs Anne Rashford.</p><p>Chueng also said the new structure would be “entirely modern, in stark contrast to the [museum’s] strict Beaux-Arts design,” and asked if there were any earlier schemes for the hall “that continued the classical expression and related directly to the historic building facades.”</p><p>The points raised in the letter echo much of the public criticism that has been leveled at the museum and its architects, RAMSA, since renderings of the project were released last month.</p><p>I've <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/09/24/griffin-msi-carbuncle-done-deal-chicago-park-district" >criticized the structure’s look</a>, size and lack of architectural compatibility to the museum’s Greek Revival design.</p><p>The two-page missive was given to me by park district officials Tuesday, following a request I made last week about the document.</p><p>Just a few hours before I received the letter, officials broke ground on a $22 million effort to convert the building’s seldom-used South Portico entrance — located on the other side of the museum from the planned Welcome Hall site — into an accessible full-time entry that would feature a new outdoor terrace, cafe, elevators and lobby space. </p><p>The building was originally the Palace of Fine Arts, built for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/10/11/griffin-msi-construction-22-million-south-portico-renovation" >South Portico</a>, which was the building's main entrance during the fair, hasn't been routinely open to the public for the past 130 years.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ed0000" name="image-ed0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/51a46ac/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F5e%2Faec2026945c8a60427452806f59f%2Fmsiportico-261013-07.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/07acc5d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F5e%2Faec2026945c8a60427452806f59f%2Fmsiportico-261013-07.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a7b081/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F5e%2Faec2026945c8a60427452806f59f%2Fmsiportico-261013-07.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. Driehaus South Portico groundbreaking ceremony.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kameron Clepper/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Chicago Park District General Supt. and CEO Carlos Ramirez-Rosa attended the groundbreaking ceremony and made favorable remarks about the South Portico project.</p><p>But afterward, Ramirez-Rosa told me the park district raised concerns last spring about the North Portico Welcome Hall design, as part of the agency’s design review process.</p><p>“Some of them were addressed through the design review process,” he said. </p><p>But the park district decided to back off after receiving letters of support for the project’s design from the preservation group Landmarks Illinois and the state’s historic preservation office, Ramirez-Rosa said.</p><p>“Ultimately, we deferred to the experts and supported the project moving forward through the city’s permitting process,” he said. “We are parks management experts. We are not historic preservation experts.”</p><p>Museum officials didn't publicly mention the North Portico project during the South Portico's groundbreaking. Museum officials previously said both projects are part of efforts to create new, admission-free public spaces and improve accessibility.</p><p>The South Portico — the museum’s largest construction effort since spending $35 million in 2005 to restore the U-505 submarine and build a new shelter for the captured WWII vessel — is expected to be completed in December 2027.</p><div entries.title: There's a lot of movement on the basketball court
entries.summary: <p>New faces heading to new places in Illinois high school basketball has been a growing trend over the last several years.</p><p>As the transfer has become so ho-hum and commonplace in the sport, it’s a challenge to track the total amount of transfers. The number far surpasses 100. But with practice officially starting in just a few weeks, here are several transfers whose impact could be felt the most this upcoming season.</p><p><i>•</i><b> Caden Crudup, Marist (from Young):</b> The defending Class 4A state champs welcome a 6-4 jack-of-all-trades senior veteran. Crudup, who averaged 10 points and eight rebounds as a junior, can be an impactful piece for a team lacking experience.</p><p><i> • </i><b>CJ Pittman, Young (Payton):</b> A steady, playmaking point guard with scoring ability switches high-academic city schools. Pittman averaged 18 points and six assists as a sophomore a year ago.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Dakari Nesbitt, Thornwood (Thornton):</b> The sophomore guard made an immediate presence last season, putting up nearly 15 points per game. He now joins a talented backcourt featuring Lester Watson and Mekhi Young.</p><p><i>• </i><b>DK Heard, King (Mount Carmel):</b> The most noteworthy local transfer. The physically gifted Heard left Mount Carmel last month. The 6-4 guard is one of the top-ranked players in the Class of 2029 after opening eyes as a freshman a year ago.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Donavyn Simmons, Romeoville (Joliet Catholic): </b>Simmons instantly becomes one of the top players in the Southwest Prairie Conference. The 6-2 combo guard has quietly been one of the bigger producers in the senior class, averaging 12.4 points as a sophomore and 15 points last season.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Elijah and Malachi Bell, Marian Central (Jacobs): </b>The brothers join their father, Lafayette Bell, who is the new coach at Marian. Senior Elijah Bell filled the stat sheet last season at Jacobs with 16 points, five rebounds and a couple of steals and assists a game. Sophomore Malachi Bell will make another jump after putting up 10 points per game.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Jacob Only, DePaul Prep (St. Viator):</b> Look for a breakout season from the smooth, long and rangy 6-3 guard after showing so much upside as a sophomore when he averaged 13 points and three assists.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Jayden and Tray Alford, Oswego (Yorkville Christian): </b>A team already returning several starters from a 22-win season welcomes the Alford brothers back to Oswego. Senior Tray Alford surpassed 1,000 career points at Yorkville Christian, while Jayden Alford is a promising 6-1 sophomore guard.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Lameck Hassan, Romeoville (Danville Christian, Ky.):</b> This is a big wild card in several ways. Hassan is a young, raw player in the junior class who moved in from Kentucky. But there is no denying his upside and potential impact at 6-10.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Mikey Woods, Perspectives-Leadership (Don Bosco Prep, Ind.):</b> Arguably the biggest arrival for any program, the talented guard began his high school career as an impressive freshman at De Sales. The dangerous downhill guard’s impact will be felt immediately.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Nate Woods, Bolingbrook (Lyons):</b> The addition of one of the better perimeter shooters in the senior class will be a boon for what will be another highly ranked Bolingbrook team. The 6-6 Woods played a big part for Lyons' 23-win team a year ago.</p>

entries.title: Bears' Caleb Williams, Colston Loveland turn up for premiere of 'Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story'
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> tight end Colston Loveland is used to getting yelled at by coach Ben Johnson, but the crew of Hallmark’s “Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story,” was even more demanding about the details.</p><p>Loveland has a cameo in the movie, which premiered Tuesday in Lake Forest and will debut Saturday on Hallmark Channel, and the job was tougher than he expected.</p><p>“I was moving around too much sometimes and messing up the shot,” he said, alluding to some nerves about his acting debut. “I’d move my shoulder an inch and they’d say, ‘Make sure you stand still.’ That was new.”</p><p>Several others from the organization attended the premiere at Gorton Center, including president Kevin Warren, general manager Ryan Poles and quarterback Caleb Williams.</p><p>Williams’ hamstring was in good enough shape to walk the red carpet, but the Bears still don’t know whether he’ll be available for their game Sunday at the Falcons. Williams posed for photos, did a video for the team in which he said it was “pretty cool” for the Bears to be featured in a Hallmark movie and left.</p><p>Getting him on board for a cameo was massive for Hallmark. The Bears are the third team to do a “Holiday Touchdown” movie, following the Chiefs in 2024 and the Bills last season, and the company wasn’t able to get Patrick Mahomes or Josh Allen for those films.</p><p>“For me, he was the No. 1 get, [but] he’s busy and with Madden and everything, his summer was pandemonium,” director Dustin Rikert said. “But he came through, and it was a real thrill.”</p><p>Like Williams, Rikert went to USC, and Williams greeted him on the red carpet with, “Fight on.”</p><p>Rikert didn’t want to spoil any surprises about the cameos, but when asked which of the non-actors from the Bears was the most natural on set, the first thing he said was, “Cole Kmet is hilarious in this.”</p><p>Loveland might want to pay attention.</p><p>He had a scene with actress Barbara Alyn Woods in which they were directed mostly to improvise, and Woods had to coach him into character.</p><p>“I feel like I drew him out a little bit,” she said. “He was being a little bit timid. I said, ‘Do what you would do in this situation,’ and then he kind of went for it. Every time, he got it a little bit more.”</p><p>Woods jumped at the chance to be in a movie set in Chicago. She grew up in Darien and went to Hinsdale South High School and Northern Illinois and has been a lifelong Bears fan. Her only complaint was that they filmed in July, and since the story is Christmas-themed, the cast wore winter gear during the blistering summer heat.</p><p>Also, she was quite displeased with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/11/bears-coach-ben-johnson-runs-out-of-answers-unable-to-ignite-offense-in-31-7-loss-to-packers" >the Bears’ 31-7 loss to the Packers at Lambeau Field</a> on Sunday.</p><p>“It sucks,” she said. “That’s going to be the only loss. This movie is going to give them confidence in such a big way that they’re never going to lose again.”</p><p>Only a master thespian like her could make that sound believable.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/13/chicago-bears-edition-of-hallmarks-holiday-touchdown-is-a-gooey-homage-to-the-city" >Chicago Bears edition of Hallmark’s ‘Holiday Touchdown’ is a gooey homage to the city</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Connor Bedard ignites Blackhawks' offense in win over Penguins
entries.summary: <p>The Blackhawks looked like an entirely different team Tuesday with Connor Bedard back in the lineup.</p><p>Bedard transformed the top power-play unit and top forward line, and the second line also delivered its best performance of the young season at the right time, helping the Hawks beat the Penguins 5-3.</p><p>The 21-year-old captain officially returned almost a full month earlier than the date range initially suggested after his left shoulder surgery.</p><p>He proved right away that he felt confident in his shoulder strength, bumping Penguins forward Connor Dewar with it on his first shift.</p><p>"I remember last year when I came back, I got blown up my first shift," Bedard said, laughing. "I'm happy it wasn't that. I'm happy I got to rub a guy out. He probably didn't feel it, but it felt good."</p><p>After that brief foray into physicality, Bedard turned his attention toward his real expertise: creating offense. </p><p>He earned his first point of the season by setting up Roman Kantserov late in the first period, delicately touching a pass into the bumper that Kantserov hammered home to ignite the power play.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Connor Bedard's first point of the season: <a href="https://t.co/pWNxolGAdz">pic.twitter.com/pWNxolGAdz</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2110170808614281307?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 14, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Bedard finished the night with that assist, three shots on goal and a 6-of-14 faceoff line in over 21 minutes of ice time. He was also on the ice for another Kantserov goal in the second period, which Patrick Kane and Artyom Levshunov orchestrated.</p><p>Any concerns about that line's lack of size — Bedard, Kantserov and Kane collectively top out at 5-foot-10 — were alleviated by their effectiveness.</p><p>"Connor creates separation a lot, so he creates space," Blashill said. "Then when the other two earn space, they’re really good players. So it’s just a good combo. </p><p>"The other thing I'd say is, Roman is very happy going to the net. So you still have a guy who will go to the net on the line, because sometimes those kind of lines get too spread out."</p><p>Anton Frondell's trio with Tyler Bertuzzi and Teuvo Teravainen scored the other three goals, including the game-winner with 4:18 left when Teravainen threw an innocent-looking puck toward the net.</p><h3><b>Pucks on net</b></h3><p>Blashill would like to see the shoot-first mentality that led to Teravainen's winning goal rub off on others. Over-passing led to the Hawks recording only 20 shots on goal despite their seriously increased offensive firepower.</p><p>"We had opportunities when we could really strike and attack, and we didn’t shoot," Blashill said.</p><p>That's something gritty forward Jordan Greenway, who surprisingly led the team with 13 shots on goal entering Tuesday, also talked about recently.</p><p>"A lot of times...teams possess the puck a lot on the outside," Greenway said. "It looks cool: 'Oh, you've got the puck!' But everyone should try to have more of a focus to get to the inside and get pucks to the net. It's not always going to be pretty."</p><h3><b>Byram’s perspective</b></h3><p>Defenseman Bowen Byram finally earned his first Hawks assist Tuesday and later got bailed out for an untimely slashing penalty.</p><p>Untimely things have been happening often to Byram — including several broken sticks in the last couple games — but his two baby girls at home are preventing him from getting too frustrated.</p><p>"It'll help me on bad days, [when] you're leaving the rink and you're maybe a little down on yourself, [if] things aren't going well — like they have been," Byram said recently.</p><p>"Some things are better than hockey and work, and it's nice to have those things to pull you away a little bit from stress and the every-day demand to perform."</p><h3><b>Line blender</b></h3><p>Blashill on Monday gave an interesting explanation of his approach to creating forward lines. For the plethora of Hawks fans upset about how often he has changed the lines so far this season, it's worth reading.</p><p>"Listen, would I like to be in the position…Vegas and Carolina are where you have 100% established lines, they don’t move them around a whole bunch and they know that those lines click? Yes, I would love to get there," Blashill said.</p><p>"We just haven’t gotten there. Three things make that hard: injuries/suspensions, new players...and young players that you don’t know what they are yet.</p><p>"I have to ride that balance of trying to get lines that make sense to us, trying to stay with them for chemistry purposes, but also be willing to change if you have to — to find that right balance for your team — without it being a blender. We’ll see where that goes."</p>

entries.title: The only gubernatorial debate between Gov. Pritzker and Darren Bailey is tonight. Here's how to watch.
entries.summary:
Taking their most direct shots yet in Illinois’ gubernatorial election rematch, incumbent Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker went head-to-head with Republican nominee Darren Bailey Tuesday night in the only televised debate scheduled before the polls close next month.

The billionaire two-term governor squared off with the downstate farmer and former legislator in a WTTW News forum that saw the pair frequently talking over each other while weathering attacks familiar from their first electoral go-round four years ago, when Pritzker beat Bailey by nearly 13 percentage points.

It marked Bailey’s latest appeal to win over Chicago area voters who soundly rejected him in a 2022 election season largely defined by his branding of the city as a “hellhole” during a televised primary debate.

“Sir, you're wasting our children's future, and it's obvious,” Bailey told Pritzker while responding to a question about education funding. “Everyone is hurting.”

This time around, Bailey has tried to pin cost-of-living increases on Pritzker, who blames President Donald Trump for most of those affordability concerns — and is keen to remind voters that Bailey is a longtime Trump supporter.

“He's sat silently while Donald Trump has taken these things away from people in the state of Illinois,” Pritzker said during a retort on Trump administration cuts to Medicaid and SNAP funding. “I think people deserve health care. I've been fighting for universal health care.”

Here are some key takeaways from an often chippy Pritzker-Bailey forum.

Trump? ‘Take a drink’

Anticipating a healthy dose of Pritzker attacks centering on Bailey’s allegiance to Trump, the former state representative and senator from southern Illinois advised viewers at the outset “to fill up your glass of water, your iced tea, your lemonade, and every time that he mentions Trump, let's take a drink.”

“It's time for Gov. Pritzker to own the failures and the problems of Illinois, because theoretically, [with] eight years in the supermajority, we shouldn't be dealing with these issues,” Bailey said in regard to federal funding cuts affecting rural health care centers.

Bailey kept up the shtick for most of the hourlong forum, chiming in to “drink up” several more times as Pritzker connected his challenger to Trump policies.

“Let's do something about the high cost of diesel in this country because of Trump's Iran war, because of Trump's trade orders,” Pritzker said over a pair of Bailey interjections in response to a question about helping Illinois farmers. “And let me be clear, Darren Bailey has cheered that on the entire time.”

‘He loves Indiana’

As Bailey highlighted the relatively stronger financial position of Indiana’s state pension system in contrast to Illinois’, Pritzker suggested his opponent’s loyalties lie east of the border.

“He always talks about how great Indiana is. It seems like he loves Indiana more than he loves Illinois,” Pritzker said. “In my view, we've got to make sure that we're doing everything we can to balance the budget in order to pay for the things that we really care about.”

“There’s a lot of people who love Indiana… they’re moving out of here,” Bailey countered.

“It’s sad, that’s what you believe,” Pritzker responded.

Bears stadium debate

The Hoosier barbs resurfaced later in the forum when the candidates were asked how far they’re willing to go to keep the Chicago Bears from moving to Indiana.

“A billionaire family owning a $9 billion valued team does not need us to buy them or build them a stadium,” Pritzker said. He reiterated he’s still supportive of providing state support for infrastructure costs, as is the case for many businesses — and bullish on lawmakers passing a bill during the veto session next month to help keep them here.

“I believe that in November, we're going to be able to get something done to keep the Bears in the state of Illinois. But I'm not going to do it at the expense of the taxpayers,” Pritzker said, drawing a scoff from Bailey.

“I'm just glad I'm not going to be known as the governor that lost the Bears. You want to know why he's going to wait till November? Because the Bears are going to Indiana,” Bailey said.

“It’s like you’re wishing for it,” Pritzker interjected.

“It's already done. [Indiana Gov. Mike] Braun's assured me of that,” Bailey said before describing his pitch to keep the Bears, which relies on payments in lieu of taxes, a concept that Pritzker has supported.

“It's a starting point,” Bailey said. “JB Pritzker doesn't have to go buy his own cars like I do… You bargain for a car. You know what it's like, he doesn't. You hear the price and then you negotiate. We've got to start somewhere, but unfortunately, that's not taking place in Illinois.”

SAFE-T Act

Bailey leveled familiar attacks against Pritzker over the SAFE-T Act and corresponding criminal justice legislation he signed that eliminated cash bail in Illinois.

“We need to repeal it, and I think we need to come back to the table. At that table, we'll have law enforcement, and we'll have the state's attorneys available because you want to know something? They were not available when they had negotiated it [in Springfield] in the dark of night,” Bailey said.

“Darren Bailey's answer to this is to go back to a system where the most violent criminals can buy their way out of jail,” Pritzker responded. “I don't think they should be able to. I think judges and prosecutors ought to decide whether or not someone should be let out in the community or not.”

Bailey interjected to ask Pritzker directly about a pair of Illinois tragedies that critics argue could have been prevented if the city had cooperated with federal immigration authorities.

“Have you even said Sheridan Gorman’s name yet? Sheridan Gorman. Katie Abraham. Can you say that?... Lives are at stake.”

Prosecutors say Gorman was killed by a man from Venezuela who was in the U.S. without documentation. Abraham died in a hit-and-run crash that authorities have blamed on a Guatemalan man without legal status.

“Darren Bailey likes to exploit people's pain for political gain,” Pritzker countered. "That is why he mentions these things… I've been fighting violent crime and making sure we have more state police.”

Data centers

Bailey took shots at Pritzker for “bringing all these data centers in, free rein, give them tax breaks, let them have their thing, and now all of a sudden we've seen our energy prices spike.”

Pritzker, who has paused state tax incentives for data center construction, said, “We should have no more data centers, unless they bring their own clean energy, bring their own closed-loop water systems, and let local governments and people living locally to decide whether or not they want a data center in their local communities.”

No sore feelings — except for excluded independent candidate

Pritzker and Bailey could be seen shaking hands and sharing some brief words as the credits rolled on their TV tussle.

But left out of the conversation was independent candidate Collin Corbett, who slammed his exclusion from the forum by WTTW based on poll numbers.

"With such a weak candidate in Darren Bailey sitting across from JB Pritzker in tonight's forum, there was no one there to hold him accountable for his failures and lies,” Corbett said in a statement.

“The truth: Illinois is significantly less affordable for working families today than it was when JB Pritzker took office. Our property taxes are the highest in the country, while our health care, energy, gas, and housing prices are skyrocketing,” Corbett said. “And all JB Pritzker does is blame Washington, while there are things we could do right now that could lower the cost of living for Illinoisans.”

entries.title: To close the death gap, hospitals must get active where patients live
entries.summary: <p>When I graduated from medical school 50 years ago, I never imagined improving health might mean building a basketball court. But after decades as a Chicago physician I have learned that healing requires hospitals to think — and listen — beyond their walls.</p><p>My teachers weren’t professors but rather West Garfield Park residents like Marquis Pitts who told Rush University Medical Center staff in 2017 that what his neighborhood needed was a community center with an indoor basketball court — a safe place for children to gather and play.</p><p>He did not ask for another clinic.</p><p>Marquis knew from lived experience what public health data shows: Chronic disease kills more residents in his neighborhood than gunfire. And that that while his neighborhood is less than 20 minutes via the CTA's Green Line ride from Downtown, residents there can expect to live nearly 20 years longer. I call this the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/11/20/death-gap-racial-life-expectancy-gap-west-garfield-park-heart-disease-cancer-homicide-opioid-overdose-chicago-west-side-loop" >death gap</a>: lives shortened by segregation, disinvestment, violence and fractured access to opportunity.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-af0000" name="module-af0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Marquis understood something institutions often miss: For people to live longer, we must listen to communities and change the conditions where they live, work and pray. No hospital can treat or build its way out of these realities.</p><p>So we became better at listening and collaborating. Wellness walks brought Rush staff and residents together. A weed-and glass-strewn vacant lot became a free outdoor skating rink. Investments followed in violence prevention, mental health services, schools, businesses and jobs.</p><p>Rush also began using its economic power differently, very intentionally focusing the economic benefits of how we purchase, hire and invest to catalyze local economic opportunity. By helping start a local company that cleans hospital gowns and sheets, for example, more than 300 West Side jobs were created.</p><p>Community collaboration led to the opening last spring of the<a class="Link" href="https://sankofawellnessvillage.org/" target="_blank" > Sankofa Wellness Village</a>, where Marquis’ idea became real. The Sankofa Village Wellness Center opened with a regulation-size basketball court at its heart, surrounded by medical and dental care, addiction services, childcare, job support, a credit union and entries.title: Remembering a mother's anguish over Our Lady of Angels School fire
entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times' Mitch Dudek's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/10/02/della-maffiola-who-pressed-for-change-after-her-son-died-in-our-lady-of-angels-school-fire-dies-at-99" >obituary</a> on Della Maffiola, who "pressed for change after her son died in Our Lady of Angels School fire," <i> </i>brought back a vivid memory from when I was 10 years old. My mother wasn’t a radio listener. But one afternoon, I came into the kitchen and found her sitting at the table listening to a news report on the Zenith.</p><p>She was sobbing, face in her hands. This was Dec. 1, 1958, and she was listening to reports about the fire. Ninety-two children and three nuns died. I asked what was wrong. She sobbed, “How can all these children die like that in school?" The radio reporter described little bodies being carried out of the building. I was aware this was a horrible news story. But I had never seen my mother cry like that.</p><p><i>Blaise J. Arena, Des Plaines</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-110000" name="module-110000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Plan discourages community investment by banks</h3><p>A recent proposal by the Department of the Treasury and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation <a class="Link" href="https://ncrc.org/new-cra-proposal-is-an-assault-on-working-class-communities/" target="_blank" >threatens</a> to undermine the 1977 Community Reinvestment Act. This proposal effectively serves as a federal disinvestment plan for housing, small businesses and nonprofits, directly contradicting Congress' recent passage of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/07/20/bipartisan-housing-bill-affordable-rents-mortgage-congress-marc-morial" >21st Century ROAD to Housing Act</a>, which was designed to incentivize community investments. Even the Federal Reserve has refused to support the proposal.</p><p>Under the proposal, 40% of banks in Illinois would lose their regulatory mandate to finance affordable housing, small businesses or local social services. Furthermore, 62% of the 81 largest banks serving Illinois would no longer be held accountable for maintaining physical branches, volunteering or investing in low-income areas. Suburban and rural community banks would have no obligation to reinvest local deposits back into their communities. This shift could cost Illinois communities billions of dollars in critical infrastructure, entrepreneurship, subsidized housing, childcare and healthcare loans.</p><p>The proposal achieves this by significantly raising the asset threshold required for a financial institution to be classified as a "large bank." By reclassifying hundreds of institutions as "medium" banks, the rule applies much lower regulatory standards. According to data from the National Community Reinvestment Coalition, several prominent Illinois institutions — including Wintrust Bank, Byline Bank, First Mid Bank & Trust, Old Second National Bank and Heartland Bank & Trust — would be downgraded to this medium tier. Compounding the issue, the proposal allows these institutions to fail Community Reinvestment Act lending metrics for homes, small businesses and small farms while still receiving a passing grade of "satisfactory" under the law.</p><p>The Community Reinvestment Act was originally <a class="Link" href="https://nonprofitquarterly.org/the-community-reinvestment-movement-ponders-its-future/" target="_blank" >born out of Chicago’s</a> community-organizing movement to combat contract selling, block-busting and redlining. Organizations like the Woodstock Institute have spent decades ensuring that banks equitably serve the communities where they operate and take deposits. Instead of allowing financial institutions to do less, Illinois residents and communities must demand that these institutions remain fully accountable and continue to provide the financial products and services required for local economies to thrive.</p><p><i>Horacio Méndez, president and CEO, Woodstock Institute</i></p><h3> A slick attempt to gut Head Start</h3><p>The outcomes from Head Start for children and their families are very real.</p><p>We see parents who arrive unsure how to access services and leave empowered to advocate for their children. We see children whose developmental delays are identified early enough to receive crucial help.</p><p>For millions of Americans, including tens of thousands of Illinoisans, Head Start is a lifeline. Easterseals Chicago & Rockford Regions partner with nearly 40 independently operated early childhood programs to deliver Head Start and Early Head Start services to low‑income families who often have no other options.</p><p>For 60 years, Head Start has helped level the playing field for these children and families. It has provided early learning, nutritious meals, healthcare, family support, resources and a pathway to opportunity for children.</p><p>But today that future is under threat.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/acf-proposes-head-start-reforms-expand-access.html" target="_blank" >A proposed federal rule</a> would fundamentally reshape how Head Start operates across the country. The proposal is being painted as a way to expand access and empower parents. But make no mistake, it would dismantle many of the nationally consistent standards that have defined Head Start for decades. It also puts significant federal funding at risk, creating budget shortfalls that states likely could not cover on their own.</p><p>A mother recently shared how important Head Start is to her family: “Knowing that my daughters are being cared for by qualified staff in an environment designed specifically to support young children gives me peace of mind.”</p><p>The long-term outcomes of Head Start are clear: <a class="Link" href="https://www.chloegibbs.com/head-start-impact" target="_blank" ><u>Children who attend Head Start</u></a> are more likely to graduate from high school, attend college, earn a college degree and achieve economic self-sufficiency as adults. Head Start provides families access to crucial resources and support systems that set the stage for generational success.</p><p>If we are serious about helping more children thrive, we should not be asking Head Start programs to do more with less. We should be asking what they could accomplish with sustained investment and flexibility to innovate.</p><p>Federal leaders should abandon any changes that would gut Head Start and reduce the programs needed to deliver safe, high-quality and innovative services. If our leaders truly believe every child deserves the opportunity to succeed, their investment in children’s lives must match their words.</p><p><i>Amy Blythe, assistant vice president of early learning services, Easterseals Chicagoland and Greater Rockford Regions</i></p><h3>Shine more light on playing politics with disaster aid</h3><p>Saturday's Sun-Times print story headlined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/08/trump-denies-disaster-relief-for-illinois-summer-storms" >“Trump denies Illinois disaster relief request”</a> deserved a place of greater prominence than Page 13. We all should be concerned when a president awards aid to Indiana and not to Illinois after the same tornado devastated towns on both sides of the state line in August. I hope this disgraceful partisanship is remembered by voters.</p><p><i>Jennifer DeFreeuw, Flossmoor</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Daughter spurns father for questionable reasons
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Last year, a lifelong friend of mine, "Lisa," succumbed to long-term cancer. I'm close to her only child, "Becky." About six months after Lisa's death, Becky's father, "Jack," informed her that he had a steady girlfriend. Becky became upset, accusing him of being unfaithful as her mother lay dying.</p><p>Becky's father clapped back, saying he had every right to be happy now that he was single, as Lisa had cheated on him years ago, breaking his heart. Becky then cut all ties with her father, including access to her three children, for saying such things about her mother. She felt he was soiling her mother's reputation to justify his new relationship.</p><p>Abby, Jack was telling the truth. Lisa did cheat on him in the past; she told me and my sister directly when it happened, so it's not just hearsay. Normally, I would stay out of any situation like this. I don't want things to get messy, and I certainly don't want to tarnish my friend in her daughter's eyes. However, I also don't want Becky or Jack to miss out on life with each other when he was being truthful about her mother's past. Please help! — <i>TERRIBLE SECRET</i></p><p><b>DEAR SECRET:</b> Check in with Becky and make sure she's OK. The past year has probably been tough for her. When the timing is right, ask her this: If her mom really did cheat on her dad, would she want to know the truth, and would she treat her dad any differently? If so, tell her what you know. If she says it wouldn't make any difference, let it go for now. You can bring it up again when her wounds are less raw.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> We are planning a multifamily vacation. Historically, we have included our friend "Rhonda" and her two boys. Rhonda has a big heart, but she brings a lot of stress to situations and is often high-maintenance. On previous family vacations, she has been difficult and would drink too much to "take the edge off." I feel bad about excluding her on this trip because of her children, but I don't want to spend an entire week with her.</p><p>Rhonda is very direct, and because she has been invited in the past, I foresee she will confront me when she hears we are going and she wasn't included. Should I proactively tell her she isn't invited or wait until she asks me about it? When this happens, do you suggest I be honest and tell her the truth? We live in the same community, and our children are friends, so she is hard to avoid. — <i>DREADING IT IN THE EAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR DREADING IT:</b> I suggest you be proactive and tell Rhonda that this year the vacation will be "family only." That way, she will be able to make alternative plans for herself and her boys. I don't think you need to tell her that her personality is abrasive or that you can stand to be around her only in limited doses. Emphasize that you need some time to focus on family bonding.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.summary: <p>Since her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/us-senate-illinois-primary-results" >primary win,</a> Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton has been building coalitions in Illinois and Washington as she challenges Don Tracy, the state’s former Republican Party chair, and positions herself to become the state’s fourth Black senator.</p><p>Although the numbers are in Stratton’s favor in blue Illinois, she says she’s not taking anything for granted. And she’s also traveling throughout the country to help boost Democrats.</p><p>“I always tell people who kind of say, ‘Oh, well it’s Illinois,’ and I always say, ‘Well I’m taking this race seriously. I am working hard to get my message out and doing everything I can..." </p><p>Stratton defeated fundraising leader U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Rep. Robin Kelly in a contentious primary that included a late campaign surge and millions in support from longtime running mate Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.</p><p>The lieutenant governor was the lone candidate to support completely abolishing ICE, offering up a more progressive stance for voters. Krishnamoorthi vowed support for “abolishing Trump’s ICE,” the same position as Pritzker.</p><p>She also made headlines during a January debate in being the only primary candidate to say she wouldn’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer as the party’s Senate leader — a position many national Democratic candidates are now taking.</p><p>Should Stratton win, she’d be part of a new class of incoming Illinois Democrats in a year that saw a seismic shift set in place by Sen. Dick Durbin’s retirement. With <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/07/30/danny-davis-wont-seek-reelection-congress" target="_blank" ><u>Reps. Danny Davis</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/05/05/rep-jan-schakowsky-announces-she-wont-seek-re-election-to-congress" target="_blank" ><u>Jan Schakowsky</u></a> and <a Dick Durbin, D-Ill., retiring, Democrat Juliana Stratton and Republican Don Tracy are vying to replace him in the Nov. 3 general election. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Susan Walsh/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“There’s a real desire to see people who are real fighters against this president, who I have had no qualms in saying has a real authoritarian agenda and wants to be a dictator,” Stratton said. “So I think it’s just that we’re looking for new people who are speaking to the issues that we care about, who are being very clear when they talk about what they want to do, the kinds of solutions they want to see that will make people’s lives better."</p><p>Stratton said while she plans to fight Trump's policies and help improve access to healthcare, she also wants to carry on some of Durbin's "unfinished business," including a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers and DACA recipients. </p><p>"I hope to carry on some of that work alongside some incredible leaders who are already doing that work in the Senate, " Stratton said. "So, not to recreate the wheel but to join in and make sure that we have a real path." </p><p>Tracy, the former chair of the Illinois Republican Party, says he’s representing the millions of Republicans in the state who want to focus on the cost of living, healthcare and taxes, among other issues.</p><p>“I’m running to bring a voice and bring hope to down ballot Republicans and Republicans throughout the state,” Tracy said. “I”ve been blessed with economic success, so I don’t have [former Gov. Bruce] Rauner money or Pritzker money. But I have enough to hopefully not get outspent 20 to one.”</p><p>Stratton had $1.1 million cash on hand at the end of June, according to Federal Election Commission records. Tracy had $1.5 million — but lent $2 million to his campaign in August 2025 ahead of the GOP primary. </p><p>Tracy accused Stratton of running a “hiding Biden” campaign — and said he wants to debate her. He stopped short of calling her a “socialist,” but said her positions align with Sen. Bernie Sanders. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.</p><p>“I guess it worked for Joe, so maybe it’s going to work for her. I don’t think she’s afraid to debate me. She’s a very good debater. She’s a lawyer, but I do think she doesn’t want to debate because it will expose some of her, what I call far left positions, Democrat socialist positions.”</p><p>Stratton has pushed back on that characterization, saying voters want to see candidates forcefully call out ICE and work towards healthcare for all. Stratton's campaign said the two will debate on Oct. 20 — and bashed Tracy for supporting Trump policies.</p><p>"She looks forward to sharing her positive vision for making life more affordable, creating economic opportunity, and defending our rights and freedoms with Illinois voters while Don Tracy demonstrates how he’ll rubber stamp Donald Trump’s disastrous agenda," Stratton spokeswoman Allison Janowski said.</p><p></p><p>As for Tracy’s view on Trump, the former Republican chair said, “it depends on the policy.”</p><p>“I’m not going to be a rubber stamp for anybody,” Tracy said.</p><p>He said he hasn’t asked Trump for an endorsement but he wouldn’t turn it down. Tracy also expressed some support for the Save Act, including voter ID and proving citizenship when registering to vote.</p><p>“I’m more of an incrementalist, and I’d go for voter ID first, and then see how that goes, and then go for the proof of citizenship,” Tracy said. “And then work on the mail-in voting rules, make it more secure.”</p><p>Whitfield Harrington Jr. is the independent candidate on the ballot and says he's helping to form the "American Center Party." He says a new party is needed to veer politics to the center. Harrington Jr. was born in Mississippi and serves as a pastor in Chicago.</p>

entries.title: What do students want from a CPS School Board president? Tune in for the debate
entries.summary: <p>Candidates vying to be the first elected president of the Chicago School Board will face hard questions Wednesday about how they plan to navigate <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/24/cps-enrollment-drops-again-amid-low-birth-rates-and-immigrant-fears" target="_blank" ><u>declining enrollment</u></a>, improve academic performance and a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/08/22/things-to-watch-as-new-cps-school-year-starts-from-classroom-cuts-to-enrollment-counts" target="_blank" ><u>pending financial crisis</u></a>.</p><p>A forum, sponsored by WBEZ, the Chicago Sun-Times and Chalkbeat Chicago, will be broadcast at 8 p.m on 91.5 FM. The forum will also be streamed on YouTube with a discussion moderated by WBEZ and Chalkbeat journalists.</p><p>In addition to the moderator’s questions, Chicago Public Schools students will have an opportunity to ask questions.</p><p>This fall, voters across the city <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/21/what-you-need-to-know-about-chicagos-historic-school-board-election" target="_blank" ><u>are electing the president, plus board members</u></a> to represent 20 geographic districts. They will make up Chicago’s first fully elected board. Early voting starts citywide on Oct. 19. Election Day is Nov. 3.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-portrait-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-060000" name="module-060000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Tune in to CPS Board president candidate forum</b><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-96a33a20-c765-11f1-92ee-5bd28bedf12c"><li>Wed, Oct. 14 at 8pm</li><li>Listen: 91.5 FM or <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/" target="_blank" >wbez.org</a> </li><li>Watch: WBEZ’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/user/wbez" target="_blank" >YouTube channel</a></li></ul><br>Who’s moderating<br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-3416ed40-c768-11f1-92d0-c77644ff26e3"><li>Kalyn Belsha, WBEZ education editor</li><li>Becky Vevea, Chalkbeat Chicago bureau chief</li><li>Patrick Smith, co-host on WBEZ’s <i>Say More</i></li></ul><br>How to engage: Our reporters will live chatting in our YouTube channel during the forum<br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-3416ed41-c768-11f1-92d0-c77644ff26e3"><li>Sarah Karp, WBEZ </li><li>Makiya Seminera, Chalkbeat</li></ul><br>Watch and share moments from the debate on Instagram Stories <br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-96a36130-c765-11f1-92ee-5bd28bedf12c"><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/wbezchicago/" target="_blank" >@wbezchicago</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/chicagosuntimes/" target="_blank" >@chicagosuntimes</a> and @<a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/chalkbeatorg/" target="_blank" >chalkbeatorg</a> </li></ul></div> </div><p>The president has the sole responsibility of setting monthly board meeting agendas, giving them the power to decide what is discussed and might get approved. The board sets policy, hires and evaluates the superintendent and approves the annual budget, as well as property tax increases.</p><p>Only three candidates remain in the race, though Sendell Revuluri, who <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/30/cps-school-board-candidate-sendhil-revuluri-drops-out-making-it-a-three-way-race" target="_blank" ><u>suspended his campaign last month</u></a>, will also be on the ballot. They are: Jessica Biggs, a current board member and former principal; Hilario Dominguez, the former deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union and a former special education teacher; and Victor Henderson, a prominent defense attorney.</p><p>The race has become especially heated and politically charged, as it’s seen by some as a proxy for the February mayoral race. Dominguez is backed by and has received nearly $600,000 from the CTU, which is a strong ally of their former staffer, Mayor Brandon Johnson, who the union helped catapult into office.</p><p>Groups that want to wrest the control of the school board and the mayor’s office are spending big to oppose Dominguez. Biggs just received big donations from two of the main players in that effort — former Rahm Emanuel advisor Michael Sacks and Paul Finnegan, a co-founder of Madison Dearborn Partners, a private equity investment firm. She’s also backed by SEIU, the union that represents CPS support staff.</p><p>Henderson is positioning himself as an outsider. He’s largely self-funded his campaign, though he has received support from a number of Black pastors and stalwarts in the Black community, like Carol Adams, former secretary of the Illinois Department of Human Services and former president of the DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center.</p><p>Each of the candidates carries baggage that their opponents have seized upon as disqualifying. Biggs was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/23/chicago-school-board-member-jessica-biggs-faces-scrutiny-over-2018-firing-as-she-runs-for-presidents-seat" target="_blank" ><u>fired from CPS</u></a> after the inspector general found she instructed staff to mislabel absent students and was put on the district’s Do Not Hire list. She got off the Do Not Hire list after winning a school board seat two years ago — a situation that has raised pointed questions from Henderson. Biggs has contended that her firing was political.</p><p>The inspector general recently <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/09/reopened-probe-into-cps-board-president-candidates-alleged-inappropriate-contact-with-teen-could-end-soon" target="_blank" ><u>reopened an investigation</u></a> into whether Dominguez hugged a minor in a way that she reportedly said made her “very uncomfortable” and asked her about her dating while working at a community organization prior to becoming a teacher. He denies the allegations and says they are politically motivated.</p><p>Henderson has had to answer questions about corporal punishment after 15-year-old divorce papers surfaced in which<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/22/school-board-president-candidate-victor-henderson-defends-disciplining-his-children-says-school-staff-should-never-use-corporal-punishment" target="_blank" ><u> his ex-wife accused him of hitting his son</u></a>. Henderson denies that he ever abused his children and says an opponent surfaced the old custody battle to harm his reputation.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-510000" name="module-510000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>More CPS School Board coverage</b><br><br>WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times have created resources to help voters prepare for this fall’s historic Chicago School Board election. Our <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" >voter guide</a>, built with partners at Chalkbeat and Block Club Chicago, is a one-stop shop to learn everything about the races and the candidates.<br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-0fd233d2-bc47-11f1-9d88-db29f813b731"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" >CPS Elected School Board 2026: Find your candidates and understand the races</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/21/what-you-need-to-know-about-chicagos-historic-school-board-election" target="_blank" >What you need to know about Chicago’s historic school board election</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/09/24/school-board-election-2026-president-candidates-voter-guide" target="_blank" >Meet the candidates for Chicago School Board president</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/school-boards/" target="_blank" >Chicago’s 21 school board races: How the campaigns are taking shape</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/09/21/key-education-endorsements-for-cps-school-board-candidates" target="_blank" >Key education endorsements for CPS School Board candidates</a></li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Endeavor Health, Rush announce proposed merged healthcare system
entries.summary: <p>Endeavor Health, including its nine Chicago-area hospitals, announced Wednesday it plans to merge under the umbrella of Rush University System for Health, according to hospital officials.</p><p>For now, not much will change for patients as the proposed merger will undergo a regulatory process that could take months before it’s approved. Once combined, the health system will include 12 hospitals in Chicago and the surrounding suburbs, which could make it one of the largest health systems in the area.</p><p>Endeavor Health hospitals include Swedish Hospital, Evanston Hospital, Edward Hospital, Skokie Hospital, Elmhurst Hospital, Glenbrook Hospital, Highland Park Hospital, Linden Oaks Hospital and Northwest Community Hospital. The hospitals will keep their names but operate under Rush.</p><p>Dr. Omar Lateef, president and CEO of the Rush University System for Health and Rush University Medical Center, said the goal is to improve access to patients and opportunities for its workforce. The combined system will include its current hospitals — Rush University Medical Center, Rush Copley Medical Center and Rush Oak Park Hospital.</p><p>“If you need a clinical trial, this should open up clinical trials,” Lateef said. “If you need access to a higher level or a more local type of care, then you can get it where you are. The goal of this is to enhance access, to take the highest quality of care and expand it to all our sites and make any patient who is in that site seamlessly able to go to another site.”</p><div Other funds will be used for Rush programs that aim to reduce the life expectancy gap in Chicago.</p><p>It was unclear Wednesday what the proposed merger will mean for nurses at Rush and Endeavor who in recent months have gone public with their efforts to unionize their workplaces, many citing concerns about nurse-to-patient ratios. Just this week, nurses at Edward Hospital in Naperville announced they had filed a petition to hold an election, a step toward unionizing under the umbrella of the National Nurses Organizing Committee.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/18/rush-nurses-unionize-celebrate-vote" target="_blank" ><u>Nurses at Rush University Medical Center</u></a> voted earlier this year to form a union under the same umbrella, which is an affiliate of the larger National Nurses United. And we’ve made very significant investments and we’ll continue to do that as a part of our future both near term and long term.”</p>

entries.title: Betty Liu’s Sesame-Cumin Chicken is double-fried for flavor and crispiness
entries.summary: <p>Deep-fry (zhà), a well-known technique where the food is fried in a pool of hot oil, which both cooks it and creates a crispy exterior, is used throughout the "Frying" chapter in my cookbook "The Chinese Way."</p><p>When deep-frying, I use a thermometer, aiming for 350°F to 375°F. Another way to gauge the temperature is to stick a wooden chopstick in the oil, and if tiny bubbles float rapidly up around it the heat is adequate.</p><p>Deep-frying often involves a double-fry technique. That method has been traditionally used in Shanghai for shrimp and fish steaks, and it works especially well for chicken. An initial fry at a low temperature seals in the juices and sets the exterior, creating a light coating. Then a second fry at a higher temperature cooks the chicken through and amps up the crispiness.</p><p>The coating here is seasoned with cumin and gets the texture from crushed sesame seeds.</p><h3>Sesame-Cumin Chicken</h3><p>Serves 4</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p>2 scallions, roughly chopped<br>3 large garlic cloves, peeled and smashed<br>2 teaspoons grated ginger<br>1 teaspoon kosher salt<br>¼ teaspoon ground white pepper<br>2 tablespoons Shaoxing wine<br>1 tablespoon sesame oil<br>1 tablespoon light soy sauce<br>1 ½ to 2 pounds boneless, skinless chicken thighs<br>¼ cup white sesame seeds<br>2 tablespoons sugar<br>¾ cup potato starch<br>1 teaspoon ground cumin</p><p><b>Cumin salt</b><br>½ teaspoon kosher salt<br>½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>½ teaspoon ground cumin<br>¼ teaspoon smoked paprika</p><p><b>Lemon mayonnaise</b><br>¼ cup Kewpie mayonnaise<br>Juice of 1 lemon<br>1 garlic clove, minced<br>Neutral oil, for frying</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Marinate the chicken: Cut the chicken into 1½ to 2-inch chunks. Combine the scallions, garlic, ginger, salt, white pepper, Shaoxing wine, sesame oil and soy sauce in a medium bowl. Add the chicken and toss to coat. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 4 hours or overnight.</p><p>An hour before cooking, remove the chicken from the fridge and bring to room temperature.</p><p>Meanwhile, make the breading: Crush the sesame seeds with the sugar with a mortar and pestle, or pulse in a food processor, until a coarse powder forms. Mix the sesame seed mixture with the potato starch and cumin in a shallow bowl. Set aside.</p><p>Make the cumin salt: Stir together and set aside.</p><p>Make the lemon mayo, if using: Combine the mayo, lemon juice and garlic in a small bowl. Refrigerate until you're ready to serve.</p><p>Fry the chicken: Heat 2 inches neutral oil to 335°F in a large, deep, heavy pot. Set a wire cooling rack inside a baking sheet, and line a large plate with a few layers of paper towels. Prepare another one for after frying.</p><p>Working in batches, remove chicken from marinade, letting any liquid drip off each piece, and place the chicken in breading mix. Flip to coat thoroughly in the breading, then set on first prepared wire rack.</p><p>When oil reaches 335°F, gently coat the chicken with more breading mixture, then carefully slip it into the hot oil. Fry for 90 seconds or until the chicken is pale golden and slightly puffy, then transfer to the second wire rack using a slotted spoon.</p><p>Repeat the breading and frying process with the remaining chicken, allowing the oil to reach 335°F between batches and using a slotted spoon to remove any loose breading from the oil.</p><p>Once the initial frying is complete, increase the oil temperature to 350°F.</p><p>Fry each batch again for 3 to 5 minutes, gently turning occasionally, until the chicken is evenly golden brown and has an internal temperature of at least 165°F. Place the fried chicken on the paper towel-lined plate to drain, then sprinkle with the cumin salt.</p><p>Serve with the lemon mayonnaise if desired.</p><p><i>Betty Liu is a cookbook author, photographer and doctor completing her surgical residency. An avid home cook who writes about Chinese home cooking on her award-winning blog, she published her debut book, "My Shanghai," in 2021, and it was named one of the best cookbooks of the year.</i></p><p><i>Excerpted from "The Chinese Way" by Betty Liu. Copyright (copyright) 2024 by Betty Liu. Used with permission of Voracious, an imprint of Little, Brown and Company. New York, NY. All rights reserved.</i></p>

entries.title: Driver dead after crashing into Near West Side garage
entries.summary: <p>A driver was dead after crashing into a Near West Side garage early Tuesday. </p><p>The 79-year-old man crashed into the garage around 6:05 a.m. Tuesday in the 2400 block of West Lexington Street, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital where he was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>The Major Accidents Investigations Unit was investigating. </p>

entries.title: Chicago Stars' Mallory Swanson scores in return to USWNT for friendly against Spain
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Stars forward Mallory Swanson didn't need much time to get back onto the scorer's sheet in her first appearance with the U.S. Women's National Team in nearly two years. </p><p>Swanson, playing her first match with USWNT since giving birth to her first child last year, delivered a powerful strike in the 86th minute of a match between the U.S. and Spain to tie things up, 2-2. </p><p>While it was only a friendly, an exhibition-style match with no bearing on World Cup qualification, it was still a big moment for Swanson and her teammates as they ready for the 2027 World Cup.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YwqveNeY7CA?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Mallory Swanson scores late equalizer for USWNT against Spain | NBC Sports"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>The two teams eventually went on to a 2-2 draw at Subaru Park in Chester, Pennsylvania. Ashley Sanchez scored the other goal for USWNT, which had to overcome a 2-0 deficit following early scores by Spain's Alexia Putellas and Salma Paralluelo.</p>

entries.title: Falcons coach: QB Michael Penix in line to start vs. Bears
entries.summary: <p>Quarterback Michael Penix is in line to start against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/14/bears-coach-ben-johnson-disappointed-in-de-montez-sweats-suspension-and-now-dayo-odeyingbo-is-out-too" target="_blank" >Sunday</a> "as long as everything goes accordingly," Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski told Atlanta reporters Wednesday.</p><p>Penix hurt his ribs late in the fourth quarter of Sunday night's overtime loss to the Ravens. He was replaced by Tua Tagovailoa, who completed two passes and then threw an interception in overtime to seal the game.</p><p>Penix, a former first-round pick, gave the 0-2 Falcons a boost when he returned from last year's torn ACL and rattled off two wins. Tagovailoa, whom the Falcons signed as a free agent this offseason, had not played until Sunday's game. </p><p>Penix is 52-for-77 for 719 yards and a whopping 104.8 passer rating this season. He's thrown three touchdowns and one interception. Penix, who was drafted seven spots after Caleb Williams three years ago, is 6-9 in three seasons. </p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Bears to make Caleb Williams a full participant in Wednesday's injury report
entries.summary: <p>Bears quarterback Caleb Williams will be a full participant when the team submits its estimated injury report to the NFL on Wednesday afternoon. While coach Ben Johnson wouldn't name him the starter, the move at least puts Williams down the road to potentially playing Sunday against the Falcons.</p><p>"It’s still fluid," Johnson said. "But I feel good about the plan that we have in place at this point."</p><p>Williams hurt his right hamstring while trying to run into the end zone in the fourth quarter of a Week 2 loss to the Vikings.</p><p>He returned to practice Friday, where he was a limited participant, and was put through a workout at Lambeau Field hours before kickoff.</p><p>"We want whoever is out there to have a good rapport with the offensive line, with the operation, with our pass catchers," Johnson said. "So, we want to make sure that we can get in a rhythm, which we weren’t able to do last week as an offense. So, sure. It all goes into account here. What do we need to do first and foremost for this week? And then a big-picture view."</p><p>Complicating matters: the Bears play two games in five days — Sunday and the following Thursday. If Williams plays Sunday, he'd have to be prepared, physically, for a quick turnaround.</p><p>Tyson Bagent took his place to finish the game but suffered a concussion. Case Keenum started the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' next game, a home win against the Eagles on "Monday Night Football." Bagent started in a win against the Jets but quarterbacked the Bears to a brutal 31-7 loss Sunday in Green Bay. Johnson wouldn't say whether he still considers Bagent the second-stringer behind Williams.</p><p>Johnson spent the week dealing with the aftermath of the loss and a new crisis. Tuesday, defensive end Montez Sweat was suspended two games for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/13/bears-de-montez-sweat-suspended-2-days-for-drug-violation" target="_blank" >performance-enhancing drug suspension</a>. Johnson said he hadn't spoken to Sweat and was frustrated by his absence.</p><p>The Bears held a walk-through Wednesday — Johnson said it was to help prepare for the quick turnaround next week — and merely have to issue an estimated injury report in the late afternoon. They'll return to practice Thursday.<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson 'disappointed' in DE Montez Sweat's suspension, and now Dayo Odeyingbo is out, too
entries.summary: <p>Not only will <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> be without defensive end <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/08/26/de-montez-sweat-says-getting-traded-to-bears-definitely-worked-out-as-he-eyes-monster-season" >Montez Sweat</a> when they play at the Falcons on Sunday, but they'll be missing fellow starting defensive lineman Dayo Odeyingbo. That's a brutal hit to their pass rush.</p><p>"We're disappointed whenever we lose a player of his caliber for multiple games," coach Ben Johnson said of Sweat on Wednesday. "Not a whole lot for me to add on that."</p><p>Johnson said Sweat doesn't plan to appeal the suspension.</p><p>Odeyingbo left the game Sunday against the Packers with a quad injury and "likely" will be out against the Falcons. Johnson said he wasn't sure how much time Odeyingbo will miss, but the team doesn't plan to put him on injured reserve.</p><p>When asked who will get the playing time in the absence of Sweat and Odeyingbo, Johnson pointed first to Shemar Turner and Austin Booker. Turner, a 2025 second-round pick, was activated from the physically unable-to-perform list Tuesday.</p><p>The NFL suspended Sweat Tuesday for two games. He will miss the Bears’ visit to the Falcons Sunday and their home game against the Patriots Oct. 22.</p><p>The suspension also voided all future guarantees in his contract, which runs through next season. That makes it financially painless for the Bears to trade or release him at any point.</p><p>Bears general manager Ryan Poles traded a second-round pick to the Commanders for Sweat in 2023, then signed him to a four-year, $98 million contract extension. He has 23½ sacks for the Bears in 47 career regular-season games, including two sacks this season.</p><p>Sweat made the Pro Bowl in 2023 with a career-high 12½ sacks, including six in nine games for the Bears. He led the team with 10 sacks last season, which Johnson said was his best overall season in the NFL.</p>

Professional Regulation suspended Johanna Morgan’s funeral director and embalmer license Aug. 5. The chapel is owned by her husband, Clark Morgan. The state accused the Evergreen Park couple of incompetent and untrustworthy funeral practices, unprofessional conduct and violating state regulations.</p><p>At a hearing last week,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/10/07/south-chicago-chapel-director-denies-allegations-over-funeral-home-practices" > Johanna Morgan denied all of the allegations</a> against her, except for acknowledging she was the sole funeral director and embalmer at South Chicago Chapel.</p><p>In June 2025 the Morgans faced disturbingly similar allegations to the South Chicago Chapel situation at their now-shuttered crematory in Chicago Heights, where investigators from the Illinois comptroller’s office found 44 bodies piled up, along with hundreds of sets of mishandled cremated remains.</p><p>The Morgans agreed to shut down Heights Crematory but admitted no wrongdoing under their 2025 agreement with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" target="_blank" >the comptroller’s office</a>.</p><p>Grieving families, meanwhile, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/30/south-chicago-chapel-decomposing-bodies-funeral-home-vigil-families" >have called for criminal charges</a> against the Morgans, even as they await word on their loved ones' remains.</p><p>Marshawna and Franquella Campbell are among those families. Their remains of their mom, Shawnese Shanned, were handled by South Chicago Chapel. The sisters attended an August vigil outside the funeral home along with their mom's wife, Alesia Williams-Shannon.</p><p>“While we have to suffer and they’re just walking around like there’s nothing going on,” said Franquella Campbell. “Just living life and we’re out here suffering. We sad, we depressed … why can’t we get the peace that him and his wife have after they put us all through hell? … Just give us our family back.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/11/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-bodies-mishandled-class-action-lawsuit" >Potential class-action lawsuit filed against South Deering funeral home for mishandling 56 bodies</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Judge tosses suit seeking to force Giannoulias, Quigley, Pappas to choose between re-election or mayoral bid
entries.summary: <p>Mayoral challenger<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/15/william-j-quinlan-candidate-chicago-mayoral-race-2027-son-richard-j-daley-corporation-counsel" > William J. Quinlan</a> suffered a setback Wednesday in his attempt to shrink the field for Chicago mayor by three: Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley and Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas.</p><p>Quinlan <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/22/chicago-mayoral-race-bill-quinlan-lawsuit-challenge" >filed the lawsuit </a>last month in an attempt to force all three mayoral challengers to make a choice: either seek reelection to their current offices or file nomination petitions for mayor. If they tried to do both, the would risk being thrown off the ballot for both offices.</p><p>But Circuit Court Judge Eve Reilly dismissed the lawsuit on grounds that Quinlan had jumped the gun. </p><p>She said the lawsuit was premature, since the week-long period for filing nominating petitions for mayor does not begin until Monday, and attorneys for Giannoulias and Quigley told the court their clients might still change their minds about running for mayor.</p><p>Quinlan served as an election attorney for leading Democrats, including in the 2012 reelection campaign of then-President Barack Obama, and as an attorney for fired former Chicago Public Schools CEO Pedro Martinez. He denied the lawsuit is a publicity stunt aimed at raising his political profile.</p><p>He argued that it is not too soon to issue a declaratory judgment, which is why he intends to appeal the ruling.</p><p>“It’s like an anticipatory breach of contract. [It’s like saying], `We agree we’re going to do this, so tell us if that’s okay,’ “ Quinlan told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“Giannoulias and Quigley could have said, `We’re definitely running. We are going to do this.’ And then, the court would have said, `Okay. Well then, this is right because they say they’re running. They’re going to file the petitions. But what they said was, `Anything can happen. We don’t even know if we’re gonna file.’ If they don’t say that, then the judge can’t make such a finding. But based upon their representations, the judge said, `I find that this isn’t ripe at this time.’“</p><p>Chicago has a long history of politicians who have run for two offices at once without being forced to choose between the two. At most, they faced a few political potshots from opponents. But that was before the election calendar was changed.</p><p>Mayoral candidates now must file their nominating petitions by Oct. 26. That’s eight days before the Nov. 3 election. According to Quinlan, that “changes everything.”</p><p>“It’s not trying to throw someone off the ballot because they don’t have enough signatures or they don’t fit the residency requirement. That’s not this case at all. This case is, we have a statute that the Legislature just recently changed. What does it mean with respect to people who are filing for two offices that are incompatible, but in the same filing period?” Quinlan said Wednesday.</p><p>“If they’re running, then it applies to them. If they are not running, then it does not.”</p><p>Quinlan said he’s “more shocked” by what attorneys for Giannoulias and Quigley said in court than he is about the judge’s decision. </p><p>“They went into court and said, `We’re not sure we’re running.’ And they say that in the pleadings, too. We don’t know. Anything can happen. We’re not sure we’re gonna run,’ at the same time they’re opening up offices” to support their mayoral campaigns, Quinlan said. “They’re saying what they’re saying in court to get what they want out of it. You should say what you’re going to do.”</p><p>But Quinlan argued that a declaratory judgment is needed to avoid what he called a “draconian” impact on Chicago voters.</p><p>“It would be draconian if we wait until after the ballot [is printed]," Quinlan said. "Any vote for Giannoulias and Quigley would be invalidated. So, you’d be stuck with the other opponent. The people who voted for them — their votes wouldn’t count.” </p>

entries.title: Public gets first peek at Metra's future battery-powered trains, a North American first
entries.summary: <p>Stepping on a Metra train can sometimes feel like stepping back in time.</p><p>The commuter railroad keeps an aging fleet. Its train cars are 32 years old, on average. Its oldest train car was built in 1953.</p><p>The feeling was different Wednesday when some Metra commuters got a sneak peek at the railroad's potential future.</p><p>Metra is showing the public a battery-powered train, the first built for use in North America, that could start running in 2028. The public can examine the machine, inside and out, at the LaSalle Street Station in the Loop through 6 p.m. Thursday.</p><p>Each single-level passenger car is painted green and blue. It has modern seats similar to those on Metra's most up-to-date quiet cars. Luggage racks, with coat hooks, span the length of the cars. There are a few tables with seating for four. The two on display Wednesday and Thursday have engineer cabs with a seat for the operator at one end.</p><p>A short car filled with lithium-ion batteries connects between the two passenger cars. People can pass through the battery car but not loiter (according to warning signs) in a narrow, brightly lit hallway similar to a spaceship interior from "2001: A Space Odyssey."</p><div
