entries.title: White Sox expect to retain manager Will Venable's coaching staff for 2027 season
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/11/the-white-sox-offense-powered-their-rise-and-its-holes-hastened-their-demise-munetaka-murakami" target="_blank" ><u>Despite a strikeout-filled finish</u></a> to a five-game American League Division Series loss to the Guardians that he admits left “a sting,” the tone of White Sox general manager <b>Chris Getz’</b>s end-of-season media availability was celebratory.</p><p>“A lot of people that followed the White Sox or tracked the White Sox, they really felt there was a team within our clubhouse; how they went about their business, how they played for each other,” Getz said.</p><p>As such, Getz isn’t interested in disrupting that clubhouse atmosphere nor breaking up the group that nurtured the American League’s best offense. The Sox GM expects to retain his major-league coaching staff for the 2027 season.</p><p>“I think about the last offseason and the amount of interviewing and hires that we made, and that certainly has paid off,” Getz said. “Now to have really talented coaches in our coaches' room, in our locker room, is something that is perhaps a separator for us, and now to really stabilize that, to have that going forward I think is going to benefit us.”</p><p>Hitting coach <b>Derek Shomon</b> and pitching coach <b>Zach Bove</b> were just hired the previous winter in a process that included manager <b>Will Venable</b> and the current front office. They likely would have been retained even if the Sox had shown only incremental improvement, rather than a 24-win jump that made history for the first playoff appearance for a team coming off back-to-back years of 100 losses or more (let alone three-straight, like these White Sox).</p><p>Venable will likely draw AL manager of the year votes, if not win the award outright, and that tends to bring some stability.</p><p>“We've got a really special manager,” Getz said. “He's got a tremendous feel for people, and his communication style and his consistency, I think allowed our clubhouse to really grow.”</p><h3><b>Meidroth going for Gold</b></h3><h3></h3><p>White Sox second baseman <b>Chase Meidroth</b> might receive formal recognition for a big reason why advanced metrics rate him as one of the best at his position. The 25-year-old second-year infielder is a finalist for the AL Gold Glove at second base, alongside Michael Massey of the Royals and Cole Young of the Mariners.</p><p>Coaches from all 30 MLB teams — including managers — vote on the award, while sabermetric defensive ratings account for about a quarter of final decision. In the latter, Meidroth rates strongly. He is third among AL second baseman in fielding percentage (.986), but first in MLB Statcast’s Fielding Run Value.</p><h3><b>Murakami talks persist</b></h3><h3></h3><p>For his part, first baseman <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> was named a finalist for AL rookie of the year in the Players’ Choice Awards, voted on by members of the MLBPA, after posting an .825 OPS and socking 35 home runs in his debut season.</p><p>White Sox fans can be forgiven for having more anticipation about whether Murakami works out a new contract this offseason, to keep him in Chicago past when his current deal expires after 2027.</p><p>“We'll continue to have those conversations,” Getz said. “Mune means a lot to us. And we certainly want him to come back here and be here for a long time.”</p><h3><b>Still seeking a Shirley replacement</b></h3><h3></h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/12/white-sox-amateur-scouting-director-mike-shirley-resigns-chris-getz-garrett-crochet-colson-montgomery-grant-taylor-jacob-gonzalez-hagen-smith-caleb-bonemer" target="_blank" ><u>After amateur scouting director </u><b><u>Mike Shirley</u></b><u> resigned in September</u></a>, Getz confirmed the team is still in the process of hiring a replacement, albeit under a modernized job title of “director of amateur acquisitions.”</p>

entries.title: Sintonízate al foro de los candidatos a presidente de la junta escolar de CPS
entries.summary: <p>Los candidatos que compiten por la primera presidencia electa de la Junta Escolar de Chicago enfrentarán hoy miércoles preguntas difíciles sobre cómo planean sortear la <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/09/30/matricula-de-las-escuelas-publicas-de-chicago-vuelve-a-caer-la-cifra-mas-baja-en-dos-decadas" target="_blank" >caída en la matrícula</a>, mejorar el rendimiento académico y una crisis financiera pendiente.</p><p>Un foro, patrocinado por WBEZ, el Chicago Sun-Times y Chalkbeat Chicago, será transmitido a las 8 p.m. por la radio en 91.5 FM. El foro también se transmitirá en YouTube, con una discusión moderada por periodistas de WBEZ y Chalkbeat.</p><p>Además de las preguntas del moderador, los estudiantes de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) tendrán la oportunidad de hacer preguntas.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-300000" name="module-300000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Este otoño, los votantes de toda la ciudad están eligiendo al presidente, además de todos los miembros de la junta, que representarán a 20 distritos geográficos. Ellos formarán la primera junta completamente electa de Chicago.</p><p>La votación temprana comenzará en toda la ciudad el 19 de octubre. El Día de las Elecciones será el 3 de noviembre.</p><p>El o la presidente tendrá la responsabilidad exclusiva de fijar las agendas de las reuniones mensuales de la junta, lo que le da el poder de decidir qué se discute y qué podría aprobarse. La junta define políticas, contrata y evalúa al superintendente y aprueba el presupuesto anual, así como los aumentos al impuesto a la propiedad.</p><p>Solo quedan tres candidatos en la contienda, aunque Sendell Revuluri, quien suspendió su campaña el mes pasado, también aparecerá en la boleta. Son: Jessica Biggs, actual integrante de la junta y exdirectora; Hilario Domínguez, exsubdirector político del Sindicato de Maestros de Chicago (CTU) y antiguo maestro de educación especial; y Victor Henderson, un destacado abogado defensor.</p><p>La contienda se ha vuelto especialmente tensa y cargada de política, ya que algunos la ven como un ensayo para la elección de alcalde de febrero. Domínguez cuenta con el respaldo y ha recibido casi $600,000 de CTU, que es un fuerte aliado de su exmiembro, el alcalde Brandon Johnson, a quien el sindicato ayudó a ganar el cargo.</p><p>Los grupos que quieren arrebatar el control de la junta escolar y de la alcaldía están gastando mucho para oponerse a Domínguez.</p><p>Biggs acaba de recibir grandes donaciones de dos de los principales actores de ese esfuerzo: Michael Sacks, exasesor de Rahm Emanuel, y Paul Finnegan, cofundador de Madison Dearborn Partners, una firma de inversión de capital privado. También cuenta con el respaldo de SEIU, el sindicato que representa al personal de apoyo de CPS.</p><p>Henderson se presenta como un candidato ajeno al sistema. Ha financiado en gran medida su campaña con recursos propios, aunque ha recibido el apoyo de varios pastores negros y figuras destacadas de la comunidad afroamericana, como Carol Adams, exsecretaria del Departamento de Servicios Humanos de Illinois (IDHS) y expresidenta del Museo DuSable y Centro Educativo de la Historia Afroamericana.</p><p>Cada uno de los candidatos acarrea cuestionamientos que sus rivales han aprovechado para descalificarlos. Biggs fue despedida de CPS después de que el inspector general concluyera que instruyó al personal a etiquetar incorrectamente a estudiantes ausentes y fue incluida en la lista distrital de personas no contratables.</p><p>Salió de la lista de No Contratar tras ganar un puesto en la junta escolar hace dos años, una situación que ha generado preguntas directas de Henderson. Biggs ha sostenido que su despido fue político.</p><p>El inspector general reabrió recientemente una <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/10/13/investigacion-de-presunto-contacto-inapropiado-de-candidato-a-presidente-junta-de-cps-y-una-menor-podria-concluir" target="_blank" >investigación</a> sobre si Domínguez abrazó a una menor de una manera que, según se informó, la hizo sentirse “muy incómoda” y le preguntó sobre su vida amorosa mientras este trabajaba en una organización comunitaria antes de convertirse en maestro. Él niega las acusaciones y afirma que tienen motivaciones políticas.</p><p>Henderson ha tenido que responder preguntas sobre castigos corporales luego de que salieran a la luz documentos de divorcio de hace 15 años en los que su exesposa lo acusó de golpear a su hijo. Henderson niega haber maltratado a sus hijos y dice que un rival expuso la vieja disputa por la custodia para dañar su reputación.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: How Blackhawks rookie Roman Kantserov is quickly establishing goal-scoring identity
entries.summary: <p>In some ways, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> forward Roman Kantserov is clearly a rookie. </p><p>The 22-year-old Russian is still amazed by all of the sights, sounds and hullabaloo of the NHL. He's still learning many of the system intricacies and even <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/01/blackhawks-roman-kantserov-anton-frondell-english-hockey-terms" >English hockey terms</a> that will become second-nature over time. He still ends almost every interview by saying, "I hope you understand me."</p><p>But in other ways, Kantserov doesn't act like a rookie at all. Examples of that were abundant Tuesday in the Hawks' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/13/connor-bedard-return-blackhawks-penguins-roman-kantserov" >much-needed win</a> over the Penguins.</p><p>Skating with one of the most famous players of his generation (Bedard) and of the older generation (Patrick Kane), Kantserov was unfazed. He was the one adding the crucial ingredients that made the line click.</p><p>He was the one driving the net, taking defenders with him to open up space for his dynamic linemates. He was the one bringing some physicality on the forecheck, forcing turnovers and preventing the line's lack of size from being a weakness.</p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill mentioned Tuesday morning his one reservation about the line was that they might be prone to over-passing, but even though that was an issue for the Hawks as a whole, it wasn't an issue for Kantserov. </p><p>He passed at the right times but showed no hesitation about shooting at the right times, either. He fired five shot attempts, getting a team-high four on goal. </p><p>Two of those went in: a power-play one-timer from the bumper position and an even-strength net-front tip-in in prototypical Tyler Bertuzzi style (after effortlessly boxing out Penguins youngster Ben Kindel).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOAL: Levshunov finds Kantserov in front, who taps in his second goal of the game. He's been fantastic tonight. <a href="https://t.co/lvDFyxQs1u">pic.twitter.com/lvDFyxQs1u</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2110180529752748445?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 14, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>In a two-game span, Kantserov has gone from pointless in his first five NHL games to tied for the NHL rookie lead with three goals.</p><p>Anton Frondell, meanwhile, leads NHL rookies with six points. It is interesting — and encouraging — that the two highly touted rookies have been arguably the Hawks' best forwards (excluding Bedard) despite the team's lingering flaws.</p><p>"Every game, I get better, and now I feel how to play," Kantserov said recently.</p><p>It sounded like the whole experience Tuesday was surreal to Kantserov; he called it "amazing that we won" against a team featuring Evgeni Malkin, Sidney Crosby and Erik Karlsson. Russian icon Malkin told him, "Hey kid, I'm so happy for you."</p><p>The fact Kantserov is already able to operate on the ice without that deer-in-the-headlights overwhelm, though, explains why the Hawks are so confident he'll be a long-term cornerstone.</p><p>Many rookies struggle to keep sight of their individual identities and playing styles while simultaneously integrating into the NHL, memorizing so many tactical details and instructions. It's a head-spinning time, and all of that thinking can override natural instincts.</p><p>As a result, one of Kane's key messages to the young Hawks has been: "Everyone's in here for a reason, and it's not to be something different than you are as a player."</p><p>"Obviously there are certain things you can get better at and certain things you can change as a player, but you can't go out and change who you are," Kane explained. "I can't go out and all of a sudden become a third-line checker, right? Like, that's not why I'm here. You've got to be confident in who you are."</p><p>But Kantserov seems to understand that inherently. The process of learning the systems — which Blashill credited him for doing remarkably quickly — hasn't blurred his identity.</p><p>That's probably because of his intelligence, which helps him not only navigate this continental transition but also complement elite players so well.</p><p>"[Roman is] so good at finding spots," Bedard said after a recent practice. "I was amazed today that, even in my head, everywhere I wanted him, he was [there] at the right time."</p><p>Said Blashill: "Some guys just really know how to feel those areas and feel that space out."</p>

entries.title: Return of the Mack? Khalil reunion with Bears makes perfect sense
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> general manager Ryan Poles has been trying to replace <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/9/5/20843106/khalil-mack-chicago-bears-2019-season-preview" >Khalil Mack</a> ever since he traded him in his first couple months on the job. It’s time to bring him back.</p><p>The Bears have needed pass rushing all season, but they really need it now that defensive end Montez Sweat is suspended for two games and defensive lineman Dayo Odeyingbo is out with a quad injury. Teams that are serious about contending make moves to patch holes along the way, and the Bears should trade for Mack in time to play him Sunday against the Falcons.</p><p>A reunion has been on their radar for a while, but the Chargers prioritized keeping Mack by shedding salary elsewhere, including trading wide receiver Keenan Allen to the Bears in 2024. But they sit 0-5 heading into their game Sunday against the Chiefs and appear primed for a fire sale.</p><p>The price for Mack should be reasonable. The Bears would be on the hook for $5.8 million in salary-cap money and have $11.4 million available, according to Spotrac. Given that Mack is 35 and on an expiring contract, he’d likely be available for a fourth- or fifth-round pick.</p><p>Mack had a career-high 17 sacks for the Chargers in 2023, then tapered off to a total of 11½ over the next two seasons. He has three in five games this season and is still in good enough shape to play 71% of their defensive snaps.</p><p>The Bears could swing a little bigger and target Cardinals pass rusher Josh Sweat (no relation), but the cost will be higher in terms of trade compensation and pay. A move like that could seem counter to Poles’ conservative approach.</p><p>Sweat, who reportedly requested a trade in March, has one sack after posting 12 last season. He has two years, $47.2 million left on his contract after this season and, at 29, probably will want a hefty extension from his new team.</p><p>The Bears are more likely to bargain shop leading up to the Nov. 10 trade deadline, so a journeyman like Commanders pass rusher K’Lavon Chaisson (one sack) could be a budget-friendly target.</p><p>But Mack makes so much sense, and not merely for the price.</p><p>He had nothing but good feelings toward the Bears while playing for them from 2018 through ’21 and is exactly the right type of player for their locker room: a no-nonsense, relentless worker who is focused on chasing a championship.</p><p>In three different transactions, he could prove to be exactly what the Bears needed at each point:</p><p>• When they believed their defense was on the verge of greatness in 2018, adding Mack solidified it as championship-caliber.</p><p>• When Poles inherited a total mess from predecessor Ryan Pace in 2022, dealing an injured Mack was crucial to correcting their salary-cap issues and restocking draft capital with a second-round pick.</p><p>• Now, at a relative steal, he can ignite a pass rush that’s been quiet since his departure.</p><p>The Bears need help immediately. They can’t wait for the trade deadline.</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson said little about Montez Sweat’s suspension Wednesday other than he’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/14/bears-coach-ben-johnson-disappointed-in-de-montez-sweats-suspension-and-now-dayo-odeyingbo-is-out-too" >disappointed to lose him </a>and Sweat won’t appeal it. On Odeyingbo, who has three sacks, he said he’ll likely miss some games, but isn’t headed for injured reserve.</p><p>Johnson mentioned that there are some defensive linemen at the bottom of the roster that the Bears “feel really strongly about,” but if that was true they’d already be playing significantly.</p><p>They’ve known all along that Sweat, Odeyingbo, Austin Booker and the rest of the group weren’t formidable. That’s why they checked in with the Raiders on superstar Maxx Crosby when he was on the trade block in the offseason, though the bidding quickly went beyond their means.</p><p>Mack almost certainly wouldn’t be available if the Chargers weren’t surprisingly winless, so that’s a break for the Bears. They can’t turn it down.</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/14/bears-coach-ben-johnson-disappointed-in-de-montez-sweats-suspension-and-now-dayo-odeyingbo-is-out-too" >Bears coach Ben Johnson ‘disappointed’ in DE Montez Sweat’s suspension, and now Dayo Odeyingbo is out, too</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Johnson's veto of bid to curtail his borrowing power survives override try — by one vote
entries.summary: <p>After an emotional and racially charged debate, Mayor Brandon Johnson’s fourth veto survived an attempted override Wednesday, preventing the City Council from making it more difficult to issue city debt by raising the threshold for approval from 26 votes to 30 votes.</p><p> Retiring Ald. Marty Quinn (13th), who championed the reform, fell one vote short of the 34 votes he needed to thwart the mayor’s veto. The final vote was 33 to 17, allowing Johnson to survive by the slimmest of margins what would have been a humiliating defeat.</p><p> </p><p>Prior to the vote, Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th) delivered an impassioned speech, accusing his colleagues of targeting Johnson because he is Black.</p><p>His voice rising, Ervin asked his colleagues, “Who gives away power?... Nobody gives away power and I didn’t come down here to give up mine.”</p><p></p><p>“Why do the rules need to change?" Ervin continued. "You want to call it independence. [But] it’s ironic that we only talk about independence and executive oversight when the person sitting up there looks like me.” </p><p>“It happened under [Harold] Washington. It happened for about fifteen minutes under Lori Lightfoot and it’s been going pretty much all the term under Johnson. Three Black mayors. And all of the sudden the rules.. become an issue. Call it independence. You want to call it reform. You want to call it checks and balances. But again, where was that concern before under Daley, under Emanuel…" </p><p>North Side Ald. Maria Hadden (49th) stuck with the mayor, saying she still “drives around the city and sees huge swaths of the city that have been neglected and just tossed aside.”</p><p>“I don’t think this change and this reform… is gonna solve our problem. I think it’s a distraction,” Hadden said. At the same time, Hadden warned Johnson that his own failure to collaborate with the City Council had all but invited alderpersons to push back.</p><p>"We wouldn’t be here having this conversation and you having to have a veto if we had better relations with Council and your office," Hadden told Johnson. “We need the fifth floor — we need you and your team — to hear these concerns." </p><p></p><p>Downtown Ald. Bill Conway (34th), a former investment banker who teaches college finance, said the notion that requiring 30 votes instead of 26 votes “will somehow delay infrastructure investment simply doesn’t square with the facts.”</p><p>“This is about the difference between borrowing to build our city’ s future and mortgaging the city’s future,” Conway said. “Our predatory borrowing of money has pushed obligations onto future generations. We are those future generations, and the bills are coming due.”</p><p>It’s the second time that Quinn has tried and failed to override a Johnson veto. The first time, the mayor vetoed a citywide ban on hemp products that Quinn championed. Though he failed again, Quinn said he made his point about the danger of borrowing more money and, increasingly, structuring the repayment schedule to postpone the day of reckoning.</p><p>Last year, the Council almost blocked an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/02/18/830-million-bond-issue-city-borrowing-costs-backloaded-repayment-schedule" target="_blank" >$830 million general obligation bond issue</a> that included a back-loaded repayment schedule that raised the overall price tag to $2 billion.</p><p>“This has been a really good fight on behalf of the taxpayers of Chicago. We’ve had some really good conversations about the city’s debt. You couple that with our pension obligations, that’s 40% of our operating budget. That’s real. It’s not gonna change,” Quinn said.</p><p>West Side Ald. Emma Mitts (37th) supported the override despite what she claimed were unspecified threats to withhold money for people in her ward affected by devastating flooding in 2023.</p><p>Without naming names, Mitts said she had been approached by “bullies” who warned her that, “If you don’t vote on this, you won’t get that.”</p><p>“One thing that I’m very passionate about is you messing with my community,” Mitts said.</p><p>The City Council also agreed to expand citywide a so-called “Smart Streets” program that uses <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/09/chicago-smart-streets-bus-bike-lane-violation" >surveillance cameras on CTA buses</a> and Chicago Department of Transportation vehicles to catch motorists parking in bus and bike lanes and provide photo evidence of those violations for automatic ticketing. The pilot program mostly confined to downtown areas has so far generated $4.5 million in parking fines. </p><p>Alderpersons also confirmed several new members for the Chicago Housing Authority board and the Board of Ethics as well two new members of Johnson’s cabinet: Fleet and Facilities Management Commissioner JuanPablo Prieto and Human Resources Commissioner Tiheta Hinton.</p><p>During Tuesday’s confirmation hearing, Prieto promised to cut skyrocketing vehicle and fuel costs by reducing the number of vehicles permanently assigned to city employees and forcing more employees to use pool cars instead.</p><p>Johnson’s appointment of Renee Hatcher, daughter of former Gary, Ind. Mayor Richard Hatcher, to succeed Mary Richardson-Lowry as corporation counsel was pulled amid complaints that Hatcher lacks the experience needed for the job.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Palatine man, 19, plotted mass shooting at Hindu place of worship, police say
entries.summary: <p>A 19-year-old man was ordered detained by a Cook County judge Wednesday, accused of plotting a mass shooting at a Hindu place of worship in the Aurora area last weekend, according to Palatine police.</p><p>In a manifesto, Alexandros Paporakis, of Palatine, wrote statements expressing white supremacist and extremist ideologies, including references to violence directed toward individuals of South Asian heritage, particularly those of Indian descent, according to police. </p><p>Detectives said they believe Paporakis may have been planning to carry out an attack Sunday, potentially targeting a Hindu place of worship in the Aurora area, Palatine Police Chief William Nord said in a statement. </p><p>Paporakis was charged with making a terrorist threat, which is a a Class X felony and unlawful possession of weapons including a rifle with a barrel less than 16 inches in length, also a felony, according to Nord. Paporakis was ordered detained by a judge at the Rolling Meadows courthouse and is due back in court Oct. 30.</p><p>On Sunday shortly after 3:30 p.m., Palatine police were contacted by Mount Prospect police about a potential mass shooting, Nord said in a statement, adding the information came from someone who reported receiving "concerning" electronic communications from Paporakis. </p><p>According to investigators, Paporakis had shared a document outlining an alleged plan to carry out a mass shooting. He also shared images depicting a rifle, rifle magazines, body armor and other tactical equipment and accessories, Nord said in the statement. </p><p>Paporakis was located and taken into custody as he was leaving his residence in the 1300 block of North Baldwin Court Sunday night. </p><p>When detectives executed a search warrant at Paporakis' residence, they found a rifle, multiple loaded rifle magazines, hundreds of rounds of additional rifle ammunition, tactical equipment, and other items believed to be relevant to the investigation, according to Nord. Among the recovered items was a tactical vest containing body armor and a patch displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism. </p><p>Over the following days with the help of the FBI, police examined electronic communications and a self-titled document attributed to Paporakis, “Why I Fought: A.K.A.: (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto),” which contained statements expressing white supremacist and extremist ideologies, including references to violence directed toward individuals of South Asian heritage, particularly those of Indian descent, Nord said in the statement. </p><p>Based on information developed during the investigation, detectives said they believe Paporakis may have been planning to carry out an attack Sunday, but a specific intended location has not been confirmed and remains under investigation.</p><p>The Aurora Police Department was also notified of the potential threat, and it coordinated outreach to Hindu places of worship in its jurisdiction to make them aware of the information, Nord said in the statement. </p><p>Anyone with information related to this investigation is encouraged to contact the Palatine Police Department at <a class="Link" href="tel:(847)%20359-9000" target="_blank" >847-359-9000</a>.</p>

entries.title: City Council OKs $260.8M settlement for 17 victims of corrupt ex-cop Guevara
entries.summary: <p>The City Council agreed Wednesday to pay a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/05/finance-committee-global-settlement-police-misconduct-lawsuits-cpd-detective-reynaldo-guevara" >$260.8 million global settlement</a> to 17 plaintiffs framed for murders by corrupt former Chicago Police Det. Reynaldo Guevara to avoid “runaway” jury verdicts that a city attorney warned could have topped $1 billion. </p><p>As bitter a pill as it is for Chicago taxpayers, the risk of jury trials would have been greater. </p><p>Deputy Corporation Counsel Jessica Felker has warned the Finance Committee that juries are unpredictable and that three plaintiffs in recent years were awarded $170 million for 42 years in custody, which amounts to more than $4 million a year.</p><p>The settlement that will resolve 16 police misconduct lawsuits amounts to nearly $680,000 for every one of the nearly 384 years that the recipients spent in prison.</p><p>All 17 murder convictions — involving events dating as far back as 1987 — were later vacated. At the time they were arrested for murder, the plaintiffs were between the ages of 14 and 28. They spent an average of 22.6 years in prison.</p><p>Forty-three people, including three women, have been exonerated after they were sent to prison on murder convictions in cases handled by Guevara in the 1980s and 1990s. Most of them lived in Humboldt Park.</p><p>The settlement in the Guevara cases will be paid out over two years, starting in 2027, in four $65 million installments.</p><p>It nearly triples the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/10/02/victims-90-million-dollars-police-misconduct-settlement-chicago-police-ronald-watts" target="_blank" >$90 million global settlement</a> that put to rest 176 lawsuits tied to former Chicago police Sgt. Ronald Watts, who was accused of framing hundreds of people on drug charges at the Chicago Housing Authority’s Ida B. Wells complex.</p><p>Ever since the Watts settlement, the City Council has pressured the Johnson administration to strike a similar global settlement to resolve dozens of remaining Guevara cases.</p><p>But Wednesday’s payout and “two more in the queue,” as Felker put it, will only resolve half of the outstanding Guevara cases. The other 23 cases will almost certainly require a similarly large settlement.</p><p>Already, the Guevara scandal is by far the most costly in CPD history. It more than doubles the $210 million in settlements, judgments, legal fees and reparations stemming from the instances of torture tied to former Area 2 Commander Jon Burge and his midnight crew.</p><p></p><p></p><p>Retiring Corporation Counsel Mary Richardson-Lowry delivered the Guevara settlement on her way out the door — and was praised for having done it.</p><p>Ald. Bill Conway (34th), a former Cook County prosecutor, has called the Guevara settlement a “gigantic, but responsible settlement.”</p><p>Ald. Ray Lopez (15th) also agreed to support the "revolting, but necessary" settlement, even though he said he had no idea "whether we actually have the money to pay for it.”</p><p>“Swallowing this is like bad medicine because I know there are still outstanding questions,” Lopez said last week.</p><p>South Side Ald. Jeanette Taylor (20th) had previously expressed frustration that Guevara, who retired from the Chicago Police Department in June, 2005, was still collecting a pension for the 30 years he spent at CPD. Felker told Taylor that a felony conviction in the scope of employment is the only grounds to deny a police pension, and that Guevara has never been charged with a crime.</p><p>Most of the exonerations in the Guevara cases came between 2016 and 2024, while Kim Foxx was Cook County’s state’s attorney.</p><p> </p><p>Johnson has been under fire for his plan to borrow tens of millions of dollars and repay that money over five years to bankroll the Watts settlement and other large payouts tied to allegations of police misconduct. No borrowing is anticipated to cover the Guevara settlement. But the $260.8 million price tag helped explain why the mayor said last month that projected legal settlements were the “biggest driver” of his projected $882 million budget shortfall for 2027.</p>

entries.title: White Sox will pursue starting pitching help this offseason
entries.summary: <p>White Sox starting pitchers logged the fewest innings in MLB in 2026, and manager Will Venable’s postseason strategy contained more bullpen games than traditional starts. So unsurprisingly, general manager Chris Getz repeatedly stated his desire to upgrade the club’s rotation this offseason during his end-of-season Zoom with media on Wednesday.</p><p>“That is not unique to other teams,” Getz said. “In our case, I think it perhaps is a little bit more pressing.”</p><p>There are a few complications to consider first.</p><p>The Sox are talking like American League Central contenders going forward. And after stunning the industry with an 84-win season and coming a win short of the ALCS, Getz’s emphasis on infrastructural improvements, adding new people to his research and development, as well as medical departments deserve attention. But even signing a single free-agent mid-rotation starter might require a bump up for a White Sox payroll that ranked 24th out of 30 MLB teams per <a class="Link" href="http://spotrac.com" target="_blank" ><u>Spotrac.com</u></a>. Getz said he has yet to have a conversation with team chairman Jerry Reinsdorf about the 2027 payroll.</p><p>Trade is also an option, with the Sox roster and upper minors holding a surplus of infielders. But negotiations take time, and MLB owners are expected to lockout the players when the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1. When this last occurred in 2021, the Sox wound up making the bulk of their offseason acquisitions during a hastily-composed spring training the following March, rather than in the opening month of activity.</p><p>“We're going to be as ready as we can when free agency opens,” Getz said. “And be able to pounce when need be."</p><p>They’ll need to figure out their internal options first.</p><p>Luis Castillo was the centerpiece of the White Sox’ trade deadline acquisitions, but struggled disastrously, recording a 8.42 ERA in nine appearances before being shut down with right shoulder impingement as his velocity waned. Castillo kept rehabbing through the playoffs and could have been an option had the team advanced further.</p><p>After a dominant first two months of the 2026 season, Davis Martin was pulled in the first inning of the penultimate game of the regular season–a loss to the Rockies that ceded the AL Central title to the Guardians–and only appeared in mop-up work in the playoffs. Martin managed right calf discomfort for most of the season, but it seemed to crest at the end of the year.</p><p>“It was very clear that he was hindered,” Getz said of Martin. “Look forward to seeing what both of those players can do for us come spring training.”</p><p>In addition to highlighting Sean Burke, Noah Schultz, and David Sandlin as rotation contributors next year, Getz expects stalwart relievers Grant Taylor and Hagen Smith to become starters “at some point in their careers,” but has yet to confirm if that will come in 2027.</p><p>With veterans Randal Grichuk and Tommy Pham hitting free agency, and switch-hitting right fielder Braden Montgomery working on swing tweaks to elevate the ball more, Getz said the Sox will also be on the lookout for outfield help. But with Sam Antonacci shifted out to left field this year and top prospect Caleb Bonemer getting center field work in the Arizona Fall League, the outfield could continue to be how the Sox address their glut of infield prospects. Getz said the team’s internal projections will weigh heavily into decisions of who to retain, and who might be swapped for pitching.</p><p>Third baseman Miguel Vargas was the team’s best overall player in 2026. Second baseman Chase Meidroth was named an American League Gold Glove finalist on Wednesday, and Getz remains open to locking up first baseman Munetaka Murakami long-term. Getz had encouraging words for shortstop Colson Montgomery, but after he set the MLB single-season strikeout record, and with Roch Cholowsky, William Bergolla Jr. and Billy Carlson looming in the minors, Montgomery has a big offseason looming.</p><p>“He’s well aware of adjustments that need to be made,” Getz said.</p>
